title: Infra team wiki - GPU fleet, Cloud Accounts, IaC & CI/CD guidance (2026)
author: Ava Martinez
body:
Summary

This team wiki page consolidates guidance for running Redwood's GPU fleet and associated infrastructure provisioning: cloud accounts, networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD for builds and deployment, and the operational runbooks used by oncall and infra engineers. It summarizes best practices, ownership, SLOs, key Terraform modules, pipeline conventions, and day-1 runbook links.

Scope

- Audience: infra engineers, platform engineers, SREs, and engineering managers.
- Services covered: GPU fleet control plane (fleet-controller), node pool autoscaler, image build pipelines, Terraform modules for cloud accounts & networking, and CI/CD job patterns that manage IaC and runtime artifacts.

Ownership

- Primary owner: infra (Infra Engineering, team: infra-provisioning).
- Secondary owners: eng-sre (incident playbooks), eng-serving-runtime (capacity coordination).
- Pager rotation: infra-oncall (see runbooks for escalation policy).

Architecture overview

- GPU fleet components
  - fleet-controller: Kubernetes operator that manages GPU node pools and rolling updates.
  - capacity-manager: internal service that tracks allocation by customer and schedules preemptible vs reserved nodes.
  - node-provisioner: IaC-backed module that creates VM instances and attaches GPUs.

- Cloud accounts & networking
  - Per-environment cloud accounts (dev/stage/prod) with least-privilege IAM policies.
  - Shared networking patterns: hub-and-spoke VPCs with centralized egress, shared transit gateway for multi-region transit.
  - Subnet allocation: GPU pools should use dedicated subnets with /24 CIDRs to simplify host IP planning.

Key operational SLOs and thresholds

| Component | SLO | Alert threshold | Runbook |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Control plane availability | 99.95% monthly | 5% error rate over 5m | gpu-controlplane-runbook |
| Node provisioning latency | 95th <= 7m | 10m median provisioning | node-provisioning-runbook |
| Autoscaler correctness | Correct scaling for target utilization (±10%) | sustained over/under by 30% for 15m | autoscaler-debugging |

Provisioning and IaC modules (conventions)

- Module layout (Terraform):
  - modules/cloud-account: sets up IAM roles, service accounts, and billing export.
  - modules/networking: VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, firewall/security groups.
  - modules/gpu-node-pool: instance templates, disk images, accelerator attachment, node labels/taints.
  - modules/iam-roles: curated roles for operators (fleet-controller, CI runners, monitoring).

- Conventions:
  1. Modules must be versioned and published in the internal module registry.
  2. All mutable infrastructure changes must go through CI/CD (see Pipelines below).
  3. Use input variables for sensitive values only via remote state or secret manager references (do not hardcode).

- Example module usage snippet (Terraform HCL):

  module "gpu_node_pool_prod" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@repo.internal/infra/modules/gpu-node-pool.git?ref=v1.3.0"
    project = "redwood-prod"
    region  = "us-west1"
    subnet  = module.networking.gpu_subnet_id
    instance_type = "n2-standard-16"
    gpu_type = "A100-40GB"
    min_size = 2
    max_size = 200
    autoscaling = true
  }

CI/CD and build conventions

- Repository layout:
  - infra/ (Terraform stacks per environment)
  - modules/ (reusable Terraform modules)
  - images/ (Packer or BuildKit definitions for GPU node images)
  - pipelines/ (shared CI job definitions)

- Pipeline requirements:
  1. Plan job: runs terraform plan in a locked remote state; posts plan to PR.
  2. Approve & Apply: apply requires at least one infra approver and protected branch.
  3. Drift detection: scheduled weekly job to terraform plan and report unexpected diffs.
  4. Image build pipelines: build GPU node image, run smoke test, publish to artifact registry, and update image variable in the IaC stack via an automated PR.

- Example CI job names and semantics:
  - infra-plan-<env>-<stack> (run on PR)
  - infra-apply-<env>-<stack> (manual/approved)
  - image-build-gpu-<family> (auto-triggered from main branch tag)
  - drift-detect-<env> (scheduled)

Networking and cloud accounts guidance

- IAM & principle of least privilege:
  - Use short-lived service account tokens where possible.
  - Bind only required roles to CI runners and fleet-controller; prefer granular role sets in modules/iam-roles.

- VPC / routing patterns:
  - Use centralized egress with NAT to control egress policies.
  - GPU subnets should be routable from the control plane (peering or TGW) and have private DNS entries for instance discovery.
  - Reserve IP ranges for node pools: annotating Terraform stacks with allocation tags helps auditing.

Day-1 runbooks (short index)

- gpu-controlplane-runbook: troubleshooting control plane pod restarts, leader election, and database connectivity.
- node-provisioning-runbook: steps to debug instance boot failures, GPU driver mismatches, and disk attach errors.
- autoscaler-debugging: investigating scale up/scale down loops and eviction events.
- capacity-incident-playbook: steps for emergency capacity increases, activation of burst pools, and cross-region failover.

Incident play and escalation (summary)

1. Triage: SRE or oncall triages using dashboards (latency, queueing, provisioning errors).
2. Containment: If control plane is degraded, route traffic to a degraded path (read-only or reduced throughput) per routing playbook.
3. Capacity ramp: run the capacity-incident-playbook to bring reserve pools online (requires exec approval for cost > $X/day).
4. Postmortem: create a confluence postmortem in /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems with impacted customers, root cause, and remediation timeframe.

Operational best practices and tips

- Capacity planning: monthly runway reports generated by capacity-manager should be reviewed in the infra planning cadence.
- Cost controls: tag Node Pools with cost-center and enforce budgets via automated CI checks on IaC changes.
- Testing: run integration tests that simulate pod scheduling with GPU requests in a dedicated staging cluster before production rollouts.

Runbook links and quick actions

- Quick CLI snippets (examples):
  - Check node provisioning status:
    kubectl -n infra get pods -l app=fleet-controller -o wide
  - Rebuild GPU image (local dev):
    ./scripts/build-image.sh --family gpu-a100 --tag prod-20260310
  - Trigger infra plan for prod stack:
    gh workflow run infra-plan-prod.yml -f stack=gpu-node-pool

Onboarding checklist (new infra engineer)

1. Read this wiki and core runbooks.
2. Get access to cloud accounts and CI; request infra-approver role.
3. Run the local image build and verify smoke tests.
4. Shadow an oncall rotation and complete the incident playbook walkthrough.

Appendix: short reference of Terraform variables and common error codes

- Common Terraform variables:
  - project (string) — GCP project id or AWS account alias.
  - region (string) — deployment region.
  - gpu_type (string) — e.g. A100-40GB, A10G.
  - min_size / max_size (int) — node pool bounds.

- Common error codes and remediation:
  - INVALID_GPU_QUOTA: request new quota via cloud console, escalate to capacity-manager for urgent requests.
  - DRIVER_MISMATCH: roll back node image to previous known-good, coordinate with serving-runtime to ensure compatible kernels.

If something is missing or you need a direct walkthrough, ping #infra or request a session with the infra-provisioning team.

Document history
